Aberdeen.region: Aberdeen and the north east of Scotland
Aberdeen.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Granite City
s1loc: Aberdeen anchors the north east visitor economy from its granite-built core. The marquee draws cluster around the harbour, led by the Aberdeen Maritime Museum in the 16th-century Provost Ross's House, the refurbished Aberdeen Art Gallery, Provost Skene's House and the Gordon Highlanders Museum. Marischal College, St Machar's Cathedral and the cobbled lanes of Old Aberdeen round out a headline set built on 900 years of seafaring and shipbuilding heritage.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Duthie Park and its David Welch Winter Gardens, one of Europe's largest indoor gardens, draw families alongside Hazlehead Park and Seaton Park. The two-mile Aberdeen Beach esplanade, Codonas amusement park, dolphin-spotting off Torry Battery and white-water rafting on the River Dee keep activity operators moving, while Aberdeen ranks among Scotland's leading golf destinations with dozens of courses.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The fishing village of Footdee, known as Fittie, preserves its cobbled cottage squares, while His Majesty's Theatre, the Music Hall and the Aberdeen Performing Arts venues fill the events calendar. The Sir Duncan Rice Library at the University of Aberdeen, the King's College chapel in Old Aberdeen and festivals such as Spectra and True North add steady cultural footfall across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade across Union Street and the West End, supported by a wide tour-operator and guide scene running out to Royal Deeside and Balmoral. Aberdeen Railway Station, the harbour ferries to Orkney and Shetland and Aberdeen International Airport at Dyce bring visitors in, with Dunnottar Castle, the Cairngorms and the whisky and castle trails of Aberdeenshire a short day trip out.

Reading.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Berkshire
s1loc: Reading carries a strong Thames Valley visitor economy. The marquee draws cluster in the town centre, led by the Reading Abbey Ruins, the 12th-century monastery founded by King Henry I, and the Abbey Gateway. The Reading Museum in the Victorian Gothic Town Hall holds a full-size replica of the Bayeux Tapestry, finds from Roman Silchester and the Huntley and Palmers biscuit story that shaped the town's industry.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Forbury Gardens, with its landmark Maiwand Lion monument, sits beside the abbey, while the Kennet and Avon Canal, the Thames Path and boat trips from Caversham draw families and walkers. The Oracle riverside shopping and dining quarter, Prospect Park and Dinton Pastures Country Park near Hurst keep activity operators and watersports centres working through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Museum of English Rural Life, known as the MERL, sits at the University of Reading, while the Hexagon theatre and the riverside venues fill the events calendar. Reading is best known for the Reading Festival each August bank holiday, one of the country's biggest music events, with the Caversham and Christchurch Meadows and the Jane Austen connections at the old Abbey School adding cultural draw.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade across the town centre and business parks, supported by a tour and corporate-events scene serving the Thames Valley. Reading Station, a major Great Western and Elizabeth line hub, and the M4 corridor bring visitors in from London and the west, with Windsor, Henley-on-Thames and the Chilterns a short day trip out from the centre.

Northampton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Northamptonshire
s1loc: Northampton anchors the Northamptonshire visitor economy with eight centuries of shoemaking heritage. The marquee draw is Northampton Museum and Art Gallery, home to one of the world's largest footwear collections of over 15,000 pairs, with its Life and Sole and Followers of Fashion galleries. The Guildhall, the round Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the boot and shoe heritage trail through the town's old factory quarter complete the headline set.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Abington Park, the town's oldest public park, and Delapre Park draw families, while Billing Aquadrome on the River Nene offers watersports, fishing lakes and holiday lodges. The Grand Union Canal, the Nene Whitewater Centre and Wicksteed Park near Kettering, one of Britain's oldest theme parks, keep activity operators and family-attraction teams working through the season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Delapre Abbey, opened to the public in its 900-year history, sits near the site of the Battle of Northampton, while 78 Derngate, the only English house designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh, draws design visitors. The Royal and Derngate theatres, the Northampton Museum collections and festivals across the Market Square and Becket's Park fill out a steady cultural calendar.

Underpinning it all is a hotel trade across the town centre and the M1 corridor, supported by a tour and events scene serving the county. Northampton Station on the West Coast route, the M1 and the A45 bring visitors in, with Silverstone Circuit, the canals at Stoke Bruerne and the country houses of Althorp and Boughton a short day trip out from the centre.

Luton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Bedfordshire
s1loc: Luton anchors a busy south Bedfordshire visitor economy. The marquee draw is Wardown House, Museum and Gallery, set in a Victorian mansion in Wardown Park, which tells the town's hat-making and lace-making story with examples of lace dating to the 1600s. Stockwood Discovery Centre, free to enter and ringed by a Medieval garden and Elizabethan knot garden, and the Mossman carriage collection complete the headline set.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Wardown Park and Stockwood Park draw families, while Whipsnade Zoo on the Dunstable Downs nearby and the Dunstable Downs gliding and kite-flying slopes pull weekend crowds. Wrest Park gardens at Silsoe, the Tree Cathedral at Whipsnade and indoor activity venues across the town keep activity operators and family-attraction teams working through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Hat Factory Arts Centre, once a working hat factory, now stages live theatre, comedy and music, while Luton Carnival, one of the largest one-day events of its kind in Europe, fills the calendar each spring. The Library Theatre, St Mary's Church and the town's lace and straw-plait heritage add cultural draw across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel trade clustered around the airport and town centre, supported by an airport-driven tour and transfer scene. London Luton Airport is one of the UK's major international hubs, and Luton Station on the Thameslink and Midland routes and the M1 bring visitors in, with Woburn Abbey and Safari Park, the Chiltern Hills and the Dunstable Downs a short day trip out from the centre.

Portsmouth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Portsmouth and the Solent
s1loc: Portsmouth runs one of the south coast's biggest visitor economies, built around its naval history. The marquee draw is Portsmouth Historic Dockyard, among the top paid attractions outside London, home to HMS Victory, Lord Nelson's Trafalgar flagship, the Tudor Mary Rose in its purpose-built museum, the ironclad HMS Warrior and the National Museum of the Royal Navy. The Emirates Spinnaker Tower at Gunwharf Quays completes the harbour-front skyline.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Southsea Common, the seafront and Southsea Castle draw families, while Clarence Pier amusement park, the Blue Reef Aquarium and the Solent watersports and sailing scene pull crowds through the season. Canoe Lake, the Gunwharf Quays shopping and dining quarter and harbour boat trips out to the forts of the Solent keep activity operators and tour teams working.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Charles Dickens Birthplace Museum, the D-Day Story telling the story of the Overlord landings and the Round Tower and Square Tower in Old Portsmouth add depth, while the Kings Theatre, the New Theatre Royal and the Guildhall fill the events calendar. The Royal Garrison Church, Portchester Castle nearby and seafront festivals run across the warmer months.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade across Southsea and the waterfront, supported by a tour and ferry scene running to the Isle of Wight. Portsmouth Harbour and Portsmouth and Southsea stations, the Wightlink and Hovertravel crossings and the international ferry port bring visitors in, with the Isle of Wight, Chichester and the South Downs a short day trip out from the harbour.

Peterborough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Fens
s1loc: Peterborough anchors a Fenland visitor economy around its medieval core. The marquee draw is Peterborough Cathedral, a masterpiece of Norman architecture founded in 1118, with its striking three-arched West Front and the tomb of Catherine of Aragon. The cathedral precincts, the Guildhall on Cathedral Square and the Peterborough Museum and Art Gallery, set in a former hospital, complete a headline set built on centuries of monastic and railway heritage.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Ferry Meadows in Nene Park draws families with its lakes, watersports, mini golf and cycling trails, while the Nene Valley Railway runs restored steam locomotives between Peterborough and Wansford. Sacrewell Farm, the Lido open-air pool and the riverside walks along the Nene keep activity operators and family-attraction teams working through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Flag Fen on the eastern outskirts preserves a Bronze Age causeway of 60,000 timbers with its visitor centre and recovered artefacts, while Longthorpe Tower holds rare medieval wall paintings. The Key Theatre on the embankment, the New Theatre and festivals across Cathedral Square fill out the events calendar across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel trade across the city centre and business parks, supported by a tour scene serving the Fens and stately homes nearby. Peterborough Station on the East Coast Main Line and the A1 bring visitors in quickly from London and the north, with Burghley House at Stamford, Rutland Water and the gardens of the Lincolnshire Fens a short day trip out from the centre.

Bolton.region: Bolton and the West Pennine Moors
Bolton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Bolton and the West Pennines
s1loc: Bolton anchors a visitor economy shaped by its textile heritage at the edge of the West Pennine Moors. The marquee draw is Bolton Museum, Aquarium and Art Gallery in the neo-classical Le Mans Crescent, with its Ancient Egypt gallery and Greater Manchester's only public aquarium. Smithills Hall, a 14th-century manor house with costumed guides, and the Grade I-listed Hall i' th' Wood, linked to Samuel Crompton, complete the headline set.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Rivington Pike and the terraced Rivington Gardens, with their ruined Pigeon Tower, draw walkers up onto the moors, while Moss Bank Park, Leverhulme Park and Jumbles and Anglezarke reservoirs pull families and watersports. Queens Park, the Market Place shopping quarter and indoor activity venues across the town keep activity operators and family-attraction teams working through the warmer months.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Bolton Steam Museum holds 30 stationary mill engines, most over a century old, telling the spinning-town story, while the Octagon Theatre, the Albert Halls and the Bolton Library and Museum fill the events calendar. The Bolton Food and Drink Festival, the Man and the Boy bronze and the town's Crompton and Arkwright industrial legacy add cultural draw across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel trade across the town centre and the M61 corridor, supported by a tour scene serving the West Pennine Moors. Bolton Station and the Manchester tram and rail network bring visitors in quickly, with the moorland walks of Rivington and Winter Hill, the Last Drop Village at Bromley Cross and the city attractions of Manchester a short day trip out from the centre.
